title: Heat Equation
body:
$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
$$

Diffusion. $u(x,t)$ is the temperature at position $x$ and time $t$, and $k > 0$ is the diffusivity.

**Read the second derivative as curvature**: where $u$ is curved upward it is colder than its
neighbours' average, so $u_{xx} > 0$ and the point heats up. Heat flows down the gradient, which is
the whole physical content, and in higher dimensions the right hand side is $k\nabla^2u = k\nabla\cdot(\nabla u)$,
the [[Divergence]] of the [[Gradient]]. The [[Divergence Theorem]] is what turns "energy in a region
changes only by flux through its boundary" into that equation.

The behaviour is **smoothing**: sharp initial data is rounded off immediately and everything decays
toward equilibrium. Solving by separation of variables gives modes $e^{-k\lambda_n t}\sin(n\pi x/L)$,
and the exponential kills high $n$ fastest, which is exactly the statement that fine detail
disappears first. Run it backwards and it is catastrophically unstable, so the past cannot be
recovered from the present.

Its steady state, $u_t = 0$, is [[Laplace's Equation]]. The same equation with $u$ a probability
density is diffusion of a random walk, which is where it turns up in
[[Random Numbers|Monte Carlo methods]] and in the noise schedules of diffusion models.
